reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive platelet function disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa), encoded by ITGA2B and ITGB3
Bleeding is of the mucocutaneous (platelet-type) pattern: epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental work
The platelet count and platelet morphology are normal, which helps distinguish it from thrombocytopenic disorders
The characteristic laboratory hallmark is absent or markedly reduced platelet aggregation to all physiological agonists (ADP, collagen, adrenaline, thrombin) but a preserved response to ristocetin
The preserved ristocetin response, which depends on the glycoprotein Ib-von Willebrand factor axis, contrasts with the absent aggregation and points away from Bernard-Soulier syndrome
Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating reduced glycoprotein IIb/IIIa by flow cytometry and, where needed, ITGA2B/ITGB3 genetic testing

Management centres on local haemostatic measures, antifibrinolytics, and platelet transfusion for major bleeding, with alloimmunisation and, in selected cases, recombinant activated factor VII considered
reference.pathophysiology: Glanzmann thrombasthenia results from biallelic mutations in ITGA2B or ITGB3, which encode the two subunits of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa). This integrin is the fibrinogen receptor that mediates platelet-to-platelet bridging during aggregation. When it is quantitatively deficient or functionally defective, activated platelets can adhere and change shape but cannot cross-link through fibrinogen to form a stable aggregate, so primary haemostasis fails despite normal platelet numbers and normal von Willebrand-dependent adhesion. The result is a lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding tendency of variable severity that does not correlate closely with the residual receptor level.
additionalDifferentials: Storage pool and other platelet secretion defects
Immune thrombocytopenia (distinguished by low platelet count)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming normal platelet number and morphology
Light-transmission platelet aggregometry showing absent response to physiological agonists with preserved ristocetin response
Flow cytometry for platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa expression
Von Willebrand studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Coagulation screen to confirm normal clotting factor pathways
ITGA2B and ITGB3 genetic testing for confirmation and counselling
redFlags: Major or life-threatening haemorrhage such as gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding
Uncontrolled bleeding around surgery or childbirth
Platelet refractoriness from alloimmunisation limiting transfusion response
reference.prognosis: With modern supportive care most patients have a normal life expectancy, though bleeding episodes can be serious and platelet alloimmunisation may complicate the response to transfusion over time.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disorder as immune thrombocytopenia despite a normal platelet count
Transfusing platelets for minor bleeds and hastening alloimmunisation that impairs future responses
Overlooking the diagnosis when aggregometry is not performed because routine coagulation tests are normal
Failing to plan peri-procedural haemostatic cover before surgery or delivery
management: Control bleeding with local haemostatic measures and antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeds and minor procedures
Recombinant activated factor VII as the first-line systemic haemostatic agent for serious bleeding and surgical cover
Reserve HLA-matched leukodepleted platelet transfusion for severe or refractory bleeding, mindful of the risk of platelet alloimmunisation
Manage menorrhagia with hormonal therapy and correct iron-deficiency anaemia with iron replacement
Avoid antiplatelet drugs and NSAIDs, maintain meticulous dental hygiene, and offer hepatitis B immunisation to transfusion recipients
Monitor for platelet alloantibodies and iron status, coordinated through haematology and transfusion services
Consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a curative option in severe refractory disease
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and screen at-risk family members
